items.prompt: Why must the body break large food molecules, like starch or protein, into much smaller pieces before it can use them?

options.label: To make the food easier to smell and taste
options.feedback: Taste and smell are sensed the moment food is in the mouth, long before this stage of breakdown happens further down the gut.

options.label: So that digestive juices further along have less work to do
options.feedback: Digestive juices act just as strongly regardless of molecule size; molecule size isn't about lightening anyone else's job.

options.label: To destroy any bacteria that arrived with the food
options.feedback: Destroying bacteria is mostly done by the stomach's acid directly; it has nothing to do with breaking large molecules into smaller ones.

options.label: Because only molecules small enough can cross the gut's lining into the bloodstream
options.feedback: The cells lining the gut are packed tightly together, and only sufficiently small molecules can pass through them.

items.ok_line: Size is the gate; nothing bigger gets through.
items.ko_line: Ask what has to happen before a nutrient can actually leave the gut and enter the blood.
items.exp_text: The lining of the gut is made of cells packed tightly together, and only molecules small enough can pass through or between them into the blood vessels just beneath. Starch, protein and fat all arrive as molecules far too large for that crossing, which is why digestion has to break each of them down into much smaller pieces before any of it can actually be absorbed.

items.prompt: What is a digestive enzyme, and why does the body need so many different kinds?

options.label: A substance that speeds up the breakdown of one particular kind of food molecule
options.feedback: Each enzyme is shaped to act on only one kind of molecule, which is why digesting a full meal takes many different enzymes.

options.label: A type of acid that dissolves any food it touches
options.feedback: Acid does play a part in digestion, but an enzyme is a distinct kind of substance from acid, and most enzymes work well outside of acidic conditions.

options.label: A muscle fibre that squeezes food through the gut
options.feedback: Squeezing food along the gut is the job of muscle in the gut wall; an enzyme takes no part in physically moving anything.

options.label: A hormone that tells the stomach when to open its exit valve
options.feedback: Signalling the stomach's exit valve is a job for hormones released elsewhere in the gut; that's a different kind of substance altogether from an enzyme.

items.ok_line: One enzyme, one job, one kind of molecule.
items.ko_line: An enzyme's job is chemical, not physical or signalling.
items.exp_title: A different key for every lock
items.exp_text: An enzyme is a substance that speeds up a specific chemical reaction without being used up itself, and each one is shaped to act on only one kind of molecule, such as starch or a particular type of protein. Because food contains many different kinds of large molecules, digesting a meal fully takes a whole set of different enzymes, each handling the one job it fits.

items.prompt: What happens to starch, the main carbohydrate in foods like bread and rice, as it moves through digestion?

options.label: It passes through the gut completely unchanged
options.feedback: That describes fibre, not starch; starch is broken down and absorbed rather than passing through untouched.

options.label: It is converted directly into fat for storage
options.feedback: Converting a nutrient into fat for storage can happen later, in the body's cells, but it isn't what digestion itself does to starch in the gut.

options.label: It is broken down by enzymes into simple sugars that can be absorbed
options.feedback: Enzymes cut the chain of sugar units that starch is built from, leaving simple sugar small enough to absorb.

options.label: It is broken down into amino acids
options.feedback: Amino acids are what protein is broken down into; starch is a carbohydrate and breaks down into sugar instead.

items.ok_line: Long chain of sugar, cut back down to single sugars.
items.ko_line: Starch is a chain built from sugar units; think about what enzymes do to a chain like that.
items.exp_title: Taking a chain apart link by link
items.exp_text: Starch is a long chain made of many glucose units joined together, and digestive enzymes work along that chain, cutting the links between units apart. What remains once the chain is fully taken apart is simple sugar, small enough for the gut lining to absorb into the blood.

items.prompt: What happens to proteins from foods like meat, beans or eggs during digestion?

options.label: They are absorbed whole, exactly as they were in the food
options.feedback: A whole protein is far too large to cross the gut lining; it has to be taken apart first.

options.label: They are broken down by enzymes into smaller units called amino acids
options.feedback: Enzymes cut the unfolded protein chain apart at many points, releasing amino acids small enough to absorb.

options.label: They are converted into starch for easier absorption
options.feedback: Protein and starch are different kinds of molecule built from different building blocks; digestion doesn't convert one into the other.

options.label: They are dissolved completely by stomach acid alone, with no further help needed
options.feedback: Stomach acid does help unfold proteins and gets digestion started, but the rest of the breakdown into usable pieces is finished by enzymes further along the gut.

items.ok_line: A long chain, cut down to its building blocks.
items.ko_line: Think about what a protein is built from, and what has to happen to release those pieces.
items.exp_text: A protein is a long chain made of smaller units called amino acids, joined end to end, and it starts to unfold as soon as it meets the stomach's acid. Enzymes then cut that unfolded chain apart at many points along its length, releasing individual amino acids and small clusters of them that are small enough to be absorbed.

items.prompt: Why does the lining of the small intestine have millions of tiny finger-like projections called villi, rather than a smooth surface?

options.label: They massively increase the surface area available for absorbing nutrients
options.feedback: That folding multiplies the area in contact with digested food, letting far more nutrient molecules be absorbed as food passes through.

options.label: They trap fibre so it can be broken down more thoroughly
options.feedback: Fibre passes through without being broken down at all; villi are shaped for absorbing already-broken-down nutrients, not for trapping fibre.

options.label: They slow food down so digestion has more time to finish
options.feedback: How fast food moves along the intestine is controlled by muscle contractions in the gut wall, not by the shape of the villi themselves.

options.label: They release the enzymes that finish digesting food
options.feedback: Digestive enzymes are released into the gut from the intestine wall and other organs, but that release isn't what the finger-like shape of a villus is for; its shape is about surface, not secretion.

items.ok_line: More surface, more absorbing happening at once.
items.ko_line: Think about what a folded, finger-like surface offers that a flat one doesn't.
items.exp_title: More surface packed into the same length
items.exp_text: Each villus is a tiny finger-shaped fold of the intestine's lining, and millions of them cover its inner surface, turning what could have been a smooth tube into something closer to velvet. That folding multiplies the area in contact with digested food many times over compared with a flat tube of the same length, letting far more nutrient molecules be absorbed as the food passes through.

items.prompt: Once nutrients are absorbed through the wall of the small intestine, how do most of them travel around the rest of the body?

options.label: They travel through the same tube the food was in, further along the gut
options.feedback: Once absorbed, a nutrient has left the gut entirely; travelling further along inside the gut tube would mean it was never truly absorbed.

options.label: They are carried by nerves running along the intestine
options.feedback: Nerves carry electrical signals, not physical substances like sugar or amino acids; nutrients need a different kind of transport.

options.label: They evaporate into the air inside the abdomen and are reabsorbed elsewhere
options.feedback: Nutrients don't move as a gas inside the body; the space around the intestines isn't part of how anything is transported from one place to another.

options.label: They pass into tiny blood vessels inside each villus and are carried away by the bloodstream
options.feedback: Each villus contains a network of tiny blood vessels close enough that nutrients crossing the gut lining pass almost directly into them.

items.ok_line: Into the blood, and off it goes.
items.ko_line: Think about what's actually running through each villus, right beneath its surface.
items.exp_text: Each villus contains a network of tiny blood vessels running just beneath its absorbing surface, close enough that nutrients crossing the gut lining pass almost directly into them. From there they join the general bloodstream, which carries them onward to wherever in the body they are needed.

items.prompt: Why does blood carrying newly absorbed nutrients travel to the liver before reaching the rest of the body?

options.label: The liver is physically the closest organ to the small intestine
options.feedback: Several organs sit close to the small intestine; nutrient-carrying blood is routed to the liver specifically, not simply to whatever happens to be nearby.

options.label: The liver processes and regulates those nutrients before they reach the rest of the body
options.feedback: The liver stores some nutrients, adjusts the levels of others, and clears out substances that shouldn't circulate unchanged.

options.label: The liver adds oxygen to the blood before it continues onward
options.feedback: Adding oxygen to the blood is the lungs' job; the liver's role with this particular blood is about processing what it's carrying, not about oxygen.

options.label: The liver removes water from the blood so it carries nutrients more concentrated
options.feedback: Removing water from the blood on this route isn't something the liver does; managing water balance is mainly a job for the kidneys.

items.ok_line: A stop for processing, before the rest of the body sees it.
items.ko_line: Ask what job the liver specifically does to blood passing through it, not where it happens to sit.
items.exp_title: A checkpoint before the rest of the body
items.exp_text: Blood leaving the small intestine's villi is routed directly to the liver through its own dedicated blood vessel, rather than joining the general bloodstream straight away. The liver processes that blood as it passes through, storing some nutrients, adjusting the levels of others, and clearing out substances that shouldn't be allowed to circulate unchanged.

items.prompt: What happens to the fibre in a meal that the body cannot digest?

options.label: It is broken down slowly by stomach acid over several hours
options.feedback: Stomach acid does not break fibre down; fibre passes through the stomach largely as it arrived.

options.label: It is absorbed unchanged directly into the blood
options.feedback: Only molecules broken down small enough can cross the gut lining, and fibre is never broken down at all, so it is never absorbed.

options.label: It passes into the large intestine undigested, adding bulk and feeding bacteria there
options.feedback: It travels through the small intestine largely unchanged, and bacteria in the large intestine feed on part of it.

options.label: It is converted into sugar by enzymes in the small intestine
options.feedback: No enzyme the body makes is able to break fibre's structure apart; that's exactly why it isn't converted into sugar the way starch is.

items.ok_line: Undigested by design, useful all the same.
items.ko_line: No enzyme the body makes can take fibre apart; think about where something the gut can't break down ends up.
items.exp_text: Fibre is built from a form of chain that the enzymes in the human gut cannot cut apart, so it travels through the small intestine largely unchanged and moves on into the large intestine. There it adds bulk to what will become waste, and bacteria living in the large intestine feed on part of it, doing what the body's own enzymes cannot.

items.prompt: Why does fat need extra help from bile before it can be absorbed, unlike sugar or amino acids?

options.label: Fat does not dissolve in the watery fluid inside the gut, so it needs to be broken into tiny droplets first
options.feedback: Bile coats fat's globules and breaks them into countless tiny droplets, giving enzymes far more surface to work on.

options.label: Fat is chemically identical to sugar until bile changes it
options.feedback: Fat and sugar are different kinds of molecule from the start; bile does not convert one into the other.

options.label: Fat is too small to be seen by digestive enzymes without bile
options.feedback: Fat arrives in large clumps, not as something too small to notice; the problem bile solves is about clumping, not smallness.

options.label: Bile kills bacteria that would otherwise digest the fat first
options.feedback: Digesting fat is the body's own job, not something bacteria would otherwise do first; bile's role has nothing to do with bacteria.

items.ok_line: Oil and water still don't mix, even inside the gut.
items.ko_line: Think about what happens when fat and a watery fluid are mixed together without any help.
items.exp_text: Fat does not dissolve in the watery fluid that fills the gut, so left alone it clumps into large globules that enzymes can only act on at their outer surface. Bile, made in the liver and released into the small intestine, coats those globules and breaks them into countless tiny droplets, giving enzymes far more surface to work on and letting the fat finally be broken down and absorbed.

items.prompt: Why does chewing food into small pieces help digestion later on, beyond simply making it easier to swallow?

options.label: Smaller pieces reach the stomach faster
options.feedback: The time food takes to reach the stomach depends mainly on swallowing and the esophagus, not on how finely it was chewed.

options.label: Smaller pieces need fewer enzymes to break them down
options.feedback: The same enzymes are needed regardless of piece size; what changes with size is how quickly those enzymes can do their work, not how many are needed.

options.label: Smaller pieces are less likely to trigger the gag reflex
options.feedback: The gag reflex responds to something touching the back of the throat; the size of food pieces already swallowed further down plays no part in it.

options.label: Smaller pieces expose far more surface area to digestive juices, so they get broken down faster
options.feedback: Breaking one large piece into many small ones exposes far more total surface for the same amount of food.

items.ok_line: More surface exposed, more digestion happening at once.
items.ko_line: Think about how much of a large piece of food is actually touching digestive juices at any moment, compared with many small ones.
items.exp_title: More surface for juices to reach
items.exp_text: Digestive juices and enzymes can only act on the surface of a piece of food, not on whatever is buried inside it. Breaking one large piece into many small ones exposes far more total surface for the same amount of food, which is why thorough chewing speeds up everything that happens to that food afterward.
